title: Tensor Products

Tensors are an odd concept, mostly because their definitions look so elusive. In our view, the easiest way to understand them is to treat them as atomic objects, taken *tantum et tale*, and to concentrate on the rules by which they combine. The basic construction takes two vector spaces $V$ and $W$ over a field $k$ and produces a new vector space $V \otimes W$, their ***tensor product***, built so that bilinear maps out of $V \times W$ become linear maps out of $V \otimes W$. We give three definitions, from the most concrete to the most abstract, and then prove that they agree.

:::definition{9.8.1} Bilinear map
Let $V$, $W$ and $U$ be vector spaces over $k$. A map $\alpha : V \times W \to U$ is ***bilinear*** if it is linear in each variable when the other is held fixed: $$\alpha(\lambda v + v', w) = \lambda\,\alpha(v, w) + \alpha(v', w), \qquad \alpha(v, \lambda w + w') = \lambda\,\alpha(v, w) + \alpha(v, w')$$ for all $\lambda \in k$, $v, v' \in V$ and $w, w' \in W$. A bilinear form on $V$ (Definition [9.1.1](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#definition-9-1-1)) is the case $W = V$, $U = k$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.8.1</span> Three Definitions

:::definition{9.8.2} The tensor product via bases
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional, with bases $e_1, \ldots, e_m$ of $V$ and $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ of $W$. Then $V \otimes W$ is the vector space with basis the $mn$ symbols $e_i \otimes f_j$ ($1 \le i \le m$, $1 \le j \le n$); in particular $\dim(V \otimes W) = mn$. For $v = \sum_i a_i e_i \in V$ and $w = \sum_j b_j f_j \in W$ we set $$v \otimes w = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_i b_j \,(e_i \otimes f_j).$$ The map $\beta : V \times W \to V \otimes W$, $\beta(v, w) = v \otimes w$, is bilinear.
:::

:::definition{9.8.3} Pure tensors and rank
Elements of $V \otimes W$ of the form $v \otimes w$ are called ***pure tensors***. Every element of $V \otimes W$ is a sum of pure tensors, since it is a linear combination of the pure tensors $e_i \otimes f_j$, and $c\,(e_i \otimes f_j) = (c e_i) \otimes f_j$ is again pure. The ***rank*** of $\eta \in V \otimes W$ is the smallest number $r$ such that $\eta$ is a sum of $r$ pure tensors. Thus $0$ has rank $0$, and the nonzero pure tensors are exactly the tensors of rank $1$.
:::

Most tensors are not pure. For instance, if $m, n \ge 2$, then $e_1 \otimes f_1 + e_2 \otimes f_2$ is not pure: if it were equal to $(\sum_i a_i e_i) \otimes (\sum_j b_j f_j)$, comparing coefficients would give $a_1 b_1 = a_2 b_2 = 1$ and $a_1 b_2 = 0$, which is impossible. We return to tensor rank in Proposition [9.8](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products).

Definition [9.8.2](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#definition-9-8-2) is concrete, and it makes the dimension of $V \otimes W$ evident. It is also uncomfortable (Harris and Auroux, in their notes on tensor products, call it ugly): it depends on a choice of bases, and it is not clear that other bases give the same space. Our second definition chooses no bases at all.

Let $F$ be the vector space with one basis vector $[v, w]$ for each pair $(v, w) \in V \times W$: its elements are the finite linear combinations of these symbols, with no relations among them. This space is enormous (when $k = \RR$ and $V, W \neq 0$, its basis is uncountable), and in it the symbols $[v, w]$ are not bilinear in any sense. We force bilinearity by dividing out exactly the relations it requires. Let $F_0 \subseteq F$ be the subspace spanned by all elements $$\begin{gathered}
[\lambda v, w] - \lambda [v, w], \qquad [v, \lambda w] - \lambda [v, w], \\
[v + v', w] - [v, w] - [v', w], \qquad [v, w + w'] - [v, w] - [v, w'],
\end{gathered}$$ for $\lambda \in k$, $v, v' \in V$ and $w, w' \in W$.

:::definition{9.8.4} The tensor product as a quotient
$V \otimes W$ is the quotient space $F / F_0$, and $v \otimes w$ denotes the class of $[v, w]$. The map $\beta : V \times W \to V \otimes W$, $\beta(v, w) = v \otimes w$, is bilinear, because that is precisely what the relations in $F_0$ say.
:::

:::note
Nothing in this construction uses bases or finite dimension. With the same relations it also applies to modules over a commutative ring $R$, which are defined in Chapter 10 (Definition [10.1.1](/notes/math-55a/10-1-modules-over-a-ring#definition-10-1-1)), where the result is written $M \otimes_R N$.
:::

The most abstract characterization says what $V \otimes W$ does, without saying how it is built.

:::definition{9.8.5} The tensor product by its universal property
A ***tensor product*** of $V$ and $W$ is a vector space $V \otimes W$ together with a bilinear map $\beta : V \times W \to V \otimes W$ with the following property: for every vector space $U$ and every bilinear map $\alpha : V \times W \to U$, there is a *unique* linear map $\tilde{\alpha} : V \otimes W \to U$ with $\alpha = \tilde{\alpha} \circ \beta$. We write $v \otimes w = \beta(v, w)$.
:::

![fig-9-8-1](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-9-8-1.svg)

## <span class="num">9.8.2</span> The Universal Property

:::theorem{9.8.6} Existence and uniqueness of the tensor product
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over $k$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. The space of Definition [9.8.2](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#definition-9-8-2), with $\beta(v, w) = v \otimes w$, satisfies the universal property of Definition [9.8.5](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#definition-9-8-5).
2. The space $F/F_0$ of Definition [9.8.4](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#definition-9-8-4), with $\beta(v, w)$ the class of $[v, w]$, satisfies it as well.
3. If $(Z, \beta)$ and $(Z', \beta')$ both satisfy the universal property, there is a unique linear isomorphism $\theta : Z \to Z'$ with $\theta \circ \beta = \beta'$.

Consequently the three definitions produce the same space up to a unique isomorphism matching the pure tensors $v \otimes w$; in particular, the spaces that Definition [9.8.2](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#definition-9-8-2) builds from different bases are canonically isomorphic. For any bases $(e_i)$ of $V$ and $(f_j)$ of $W$, the pure tensors $e_i \otimes f_j$ form a basis of $V \otimes W$, and $\dim(V \otimes W) = (\dim V)(\dim W)$.
:::

:::proof
(i) Let $\alpha : V \times W \to U$ be bilinear, and let $\tilde{\alpha}$ be the linear map with $\tilde{\alpha}(e_i \otimes f_j) = \alpha(e_i, f_j)$ (a linear map may take arbitrary values on a basis). For $v = \sum_i a_i e_i$ and $w = \sum_j b_j f_j$, bilinearity gives $$\alpha(v, w) = \sum_{i,j} a_i b_j\, \alpha(e_i, f_j) = \tilde{\alpha}\Big(\sum_{i,j} a_i b_j\, e_i \otimes f_j\Big) = \tilde{\alpha}(v \otimes w).$$ Any linear map $\psi$ with $\psi \circ \beta = \alpha$ satisfies $\psi(e_i \otimes f_j) = \alpha(e_i, f_j)$, so $\psi = \tilde{\alpha}$, because a linear map is determined by its values on a basis.

(ii) Given $\alpha$, let $\psi : F \to U$ be the linear map with $\psi([v, w]) = \alpha(v, w)$. Each spanning element of $F_0$ maps to $0$ because $\alpha$ is bilinear; for example, $\psi([\lambda v, w] - \lambda [v, w]) = \alpha(\lambda v, w) - \lambda \alpha(v, w) = 0$. So $F_0 \subseteq \ker \psi$, and by the universal property of the quotient space (Theorem [7.1.7](/notes/math-55a/7-1-quotient-spaces#theorem-7-1-7)), $\psi$ factors through a linear map $\tilde{\alpha} : F/F_0 \to U$ with $\tilde{\alpha}(v \otimes w) = \alpha(v, w)$. It is unique because the classes $v \otimes w$ span $F/F_0$.

(iii) The universal property of $(Z, \beta)$, applied to the bilinear map $\beta'$, gives a linear map $\theta : Z \to Z'$ with $\theta \circ \beta = \beta'$, and it is the only such map. Symmetrically there is $\theta' : Z' \to Z$ with $\theta' \circ \beta' = \beta$. Then $\theta' \circ \theta : Z \to Z$ is linear and $(\theta' \circ \theta) \circ \beta = \beta$; the identity of $Z$ has the same property, so the uniqueness in the universal property of $(Z, \beta)$, applied to $\alpha = \beta$, gives $\theta' \circ \theta = \id_Z$. Likewise $\theta \circ \theta' = \id_{Z'}$.

For the last statements: by (i)–(iii), any model $Z$ of the tensor product is isomorphic to the space built in Definition [9.8.2](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#definition-9-8-2) from the bases $(e_i)$ and $(f_j)$, by an isomorphism matching pure tensors. That isomorphism carries the basis $(e_i \otimes f_j)$ of the latter to the elements $e_i \otimes f_j$ of $Z$, which therefore form a basis of $Z$.
:::

:::note
The argument in (iii) applies to every object defined by a universal property, as for products and coproducts (Section [8.3](/notes/math-55a/8-3-universal-properties)): the universal property determines the object up to unique isomorphism, and a separate construction shows that it exists. From now on $V \otimes W$ means any of these spaces, and we use whichever description is convenient. In practice, two facts get used constantly: to define a linear map out of $V \otimes W$, it suffices to give a bilinear map out of $V \times W$; and two linear maps out of $V \otimes W$ that agree on all pure tensors are equal, because pure tensors span.
:::

:::note
The assignment $\alpha \mapsto \tilde{\alpha}$ is a bijection from the bilinear maps $V \times W \to U$ to the linear maps $V \otimes W \to U$, with inverse $\psi \mapsto \psi \circ \beta$. It is linear, so it identifies the vector space of bilinear maps $V \times W \to U$ with $\Hom(V \otimes W, U)$. In this sense the tensor product converts bilinear problems into linear ones.
:::

## <span class="num">9.8.3</span> Functoriality and Basic Identities

:::proposition{9.8.7} Tensor product of linear maps
Let $\varphi : V \to V'$ and $\psi : W \to W'$ be linear maps between finite-dimensional vector spaces. There is a unique linear map $\varphi \otimes \psi : V \otimes W \to V' \otimes W'$ with $$(\varphi \otimes \psi)(v \otimes w) = \varphi(v) \otimes \psi(w).$$ Moreover:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $(\varphi' \circ \varphi) \otimes (\psi' \circ \psi) = (\varphi' \otimes \psi') \circ (\varphi \otimes \psi)$ for linear maps $\varphi' : V' \to V''$, $\psi' : W' \to W''$, and $\id_V \otimes \id_W = \id_{V \otimes W}$;
2. if $V' = V$ and $W' = W$, then $\Tr(\varphi \otimes \psi) = \Tr(\varphi)\,\Tr(\psi)$.
:::

:::proof
The map $V \times W \to V' \otimes W'$, $(v, w) \mapsto \varphi(v) \otimes \psi(w)$, is bilinear, because $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are linear and $\otimes$ is bilinear. By the universal property it induces a unique linear map $\varphi \otimes \psi$ with the stated values.

(i) On pure tensors, $$((\varphi' \otimes \psi') \circ (\varphi \otimes \psi))(v \otimes w) = \varphi'(\varphi(v)) \otimes \psi'(\psi(w)) = ((\varphi' \circ \varphi) \otimes (\psi' \circ \psi))(v \otimes w),$$ and two linear maps that agree on pure tensors are equal. The same argument gives $\id_V \otimes \id_W = \id_{V \otimes W}$.

(ii) Let $A = (a_{ki})$ and $B = (b_{lj})$ be the matrices of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ in bases $(e_i)$ of $V$ and $(f_j)$ of $W$. Then $$(\varphi \otimes \psi)(e_i \otimes f_j) = \varphi(e_i) \otimes \psi(f_j) = \sum_{k,l} a_{ki} b_{lj}\, e_k \otimes f_l,$$ so the diagonal entry of the matrix of $\varphi \otimes \psi$ at $e_i \otimes f_j$ is $a_{ii} b_{jj}$. Hence $\Tr(\varphi \otimes \psi) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ii} b_{jj} = \Tr(A)\,\Tr(B)$.
:::

In the language of Definition [8.2.1](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#definition-8-2-1), part (i) says that $\otimes$ is a functor in two variables: it is a functor in each variable when the other is held fixed, and the two variables do not interfere. In particular, if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are isomorphisms, so is $\varphi \otimes \psi$, with inverse $\varphi^{-1} \otimes \psi^{-1}$.

:::proposition{9.8.8} Basic identities
Let $U$, $V$, $W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over $k$. There are isomorphisms

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $V \otimes W \cong W \otimes V$, with $v \otimes w \mapsto w \otimes v$;
2. $(U \oplus V) \otimes W \cong (U \otimes W) \oplus (V \otimes W)$, with $(u, v) \otimes w \mapsto (u \otimes w, v \otimes w)$;
3. $k \otimes V \cong V$, with $\lambda \otimes v \mapsto \lambda v$.
:::

:::proof
In each case the formula comes from a bilinear map on the product of the two factors, namely $(v, w) \mapsto w \otimes v$, $((u, v), w) \mapsto (u \otimes w, v \otimes w)$ and $(\lambda, v) \mapsto \lambda v$. By the universal property each induces a linear map with the stated values on pure tensors. Each of these maps sends a basis to a basis, so it is an isomorphism. Indeed, let $(g_l)$, $(e_i)$, $(f_j)$ be bases of $U$, $V$, $W$. In (i), $e_i \otimes f_j \mapsto f_j \otimes e_i$. In (ii), the vectors $(g_l, 0)$ and $(0, e_i)$ form a basis of $U \oplus V$, and $(g_l, 0) \otimes f_j \mapsto (g_l \otimes f_j, 0)$, $(0, e_i) \otimes f_j \mapsto (0, e_i \otimes f_j)$, which together form a basis of $(U \otimes W) \oplus (V \otimes W)$. In (iii), $1 \otimes e_i \mapsto e_i$.
:::

:::example{9.8.9} Complexification as a tensor product
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and regard $\CC$ as a real vector space with basis $1, i$. Write $V \otimes_{\RR} \CC$ for the tensor product of these two real vector spaces. For $\lambda \in \CC$, multiplication by $\lambda$ is an $\RR$-linear map $m_\lambda : \CC \to \CC$, and we set $\lambda \cdot \xi = (\id_V \otimes m_\lambda)(\xi)$, so that $\lambda \cdot (v \otimes z) = v \otimes \lambda z$. Proposition [9.8.7](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-7)(i) gives $(\lambda\mu) \cdot \xi = \lambda \cdot (\mu \cdot \xi)$ and $1 \cdot \xi = \xi$, and checking on pure tensors gives the distributive laws; so $V \otimes_{\RR} \CC$ is a complex vector space.

If $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis of $V$, the vectors $e_j \otimes 1$, $e_j \otimes i$ form a real basis of $V \otimes_{\RR} \CC$, and $e_j \otimes i = i \cdot (e_j \otimes 1)$, so the $e_j \otimes 1$ form a complex basis. The map from the complexification $V_{\CC}$ of Definition [7.10.1](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification#definition-7-10-1), $$V_{\CC} \to V \otimes_{\RR} \CC, \qquad v + iw \mapsto v \otimes 1 + w \otimes i,$$ is $\RR$-linear and sends a real basis to a real basis. It also commutes with multiplication by $i$: the vector $i(v + iw) = -w + iv$ goes to $-w \otimes 1 + v \otimes i = i \cdot (v \otimes 1 + w \otimes i)$. So it is an isomorphism of complex vector spaces, and under it $\varphi_{\CC}$ corresponds to $\varphi \otimes \id_{\CC}$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.8.4</span> Hom as a Tensor Product

The most useful identity involving tensor products is the following. For a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$ we write $e_1^*, \ldots, e_n^*$ for the dual basis of $V^*$ (Definition [6.2.5](/notes/math-55a/6-2-duality#definition-6-2-5)), so $e_i^*(e_j) = \delta_{ij}$.

:::proposition{9.8.10} $\Hom(V, W) \cong V^* \otimes W$
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional. There is an isomorphism $$\Phi : V^* \otimes W \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Hom(V, W), \qquad \Phi(\ell \otimes w) = \big(v \mapsto \ell(v)\, w\big),$$ defined without any choice of bases. It is compatible with composition: for linear maps $\alpha : V' \to V$ and $\gamma : W \to W'$ between finite-dimensional spaces, $$\gamma \circ \Phi(\eta) \circ \alpha = \Phi\big((\alpha^t \otimes \gamma)(\eta)\big) \qquad \text{for all } \eta \in V^* \otimes W,$$ where $\alpha^t : V^* \to V'^*$ is the dual map (Definition [6.2.9](/notes/math-55a/6-2-duality#definition-6-2-9)).
:::

:::proof
The map $V^* \times W \to \Hom(V, W)$, $(\ell, w) \mapsto (v \mapsto \ell(v) w)$, is bilinear: $(\lambda \ell + \ell')(v)\, w = \lambda\, \ell(v) w + \ell'(v) w$, and similarly in $w$. By the universal property it induces a linear map $\Phi$ with the stated values.

Choose bases $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$ and $f_1, \ldots, f_m$ of $W$. The map $\Phi(e_i^* \otimes f_j)$ sends $e_i$ to $f_j$ and every other $e_k$ to $0$, so its matrix is the $m \times n$ matrix with a $1$ in row $j$, column $i$, and zeros elsewhere. These $mn$ matrices form a basis of the space of $m \times n$ matrices, which is isomorphic to $\Hom(V, W)$ by taking matrices in the chosen bases (Theorem [5.2.7](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#theorem-5-2-7)). So $\Phi$ sends the basis $(e_i^* \otimes f_j)$ of $V^* \otimes W$ to a basis of $\Hom(V, W)$, and it is an isomorphism.

Both sides of the compatibility formula are linear in $\eta$, so it suffices to check it for $\eta = \ell \otimes w$. For $v' \in V'$, $$\gamma\big(\Phi(\ell \otimes w)(\alpha(v'))\big) = \ell(\alpha(v'))\, \gamma(w) = (\alpha^t \ell)(v')\, \gamma(w) = \Phi\big(\alpha^t \ell \otimes \gamma(w)\big)(v').$$
:::

Under $\Phi$, a pure tensor $\ell \otimes w$ with $\ell \neq 0$ and $w \neq 0$ is the map $v \mapsto \ell(v) w$, whose image is the line spanned by $w$: a map of rank one. This is the first case of a general fact, which explains the name “rank” for tensors.

:::proposition{9.8.11} Tensor rank equals rank
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional and $\eta \in V^* \otimes W$. The rank of $\eta$ as a tensor equals the rank of the linear map $\Phi(\eta) : V \to W$.
:::

:::proof
Let $r$ be the tensor rank of $\eta$ and $\varphi = \Phi(\eta)$. If $\eta = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ell_i \otimes w_i$, then $\varphi(v) = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ell_i(v)\, w_i$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(w_1, \ldots, w_r)$ for every $v$, so $\rank \varphi \le r$.

Conversely, let $s = \rank \varphi$ and $n = \dim V$. By the Rank–Nullity Theorem (Theorem [6.1.12](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#theorem-6-1-12)), $\dim \ker \varphi = n - s$. Choose a basis $e_{s+1}, \ldots, e_n$ of $\ker \varphi$, extend it to a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$, and let $(e_i^*)$ be the dual basis. The map $\Phi\big(\sum_{i=1}^{s} e_i^* \otimes \varphi(e_i)\big)$ sends $e_j$ to $\varphi(e_j)$ for $j \le s$ and to $0 = \varphi(e_j)$ for $j > s$, so it equals $\varphi$. Since $\Phi$ is injective, $\eta = \sum_{i=1}^{s} e_i^* \otimes \varphi(e_i)$, a sum of $s$ pure tensors, and $r \le s$.
:::

:::example{9.8.12} A $2 \times 2$ matrix as a tensor
Let $V$ and $W$ have bases $e_1, e_2$ and $f_1, f_2$. The linear map with matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ sends $e_1 \mapsto a f_1 + c f_2$ and $e_2 \mapsto b f_1 + d f_2$, so it corresponds under $\Phi$ to the tensor $$e_1^* \otimes (a f_1 + c f_2) + e_2^* \otimes (b f_1 + d f_2).$$ By Proposition [9.8.11](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-11), this tensor is pure exactly when the matrix has rank at most $1$, that is, when its columns are proportional, that is, when $ad - bc = 0$. Otherwise it has rank $2$.
:::

:::proposition{9.8.13} Duals and bilinear forms
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. There is an isomorphism $V^* \otimes W^* \to (V \otimes W)^*$ sending $\ell \otimes m$ to the linear functional with $v \otimes w \mapsto \ell(v)\, m(w)$.
2. The space $B(V)$ of bilinear forms on $V$ is isomorphic to $V^* \otimes V^*$; the tensor $\ell \otimes m$ corresponds to the form $b(v, w) = \ell(v)\, m(w)$.
:::

:::proof
(i) For fixed $(\ell, m)$, the map $(v, w) \mapsto \ell(v) m(w)$ is bilinear, so it induces a linear functional on $V \otimes W$. Its values on pure tensors depend bilinearly on $(\ell, m)$, and pure tensors span, so the functional itself depends bilinearly on $(\ell, m)$; the universal property gives a linear map $V^* \otimes W^* \to (V \otimes W)^*$. With bases $(e_i)$ of $V$ and $(f_j)$ of $W$, it sends $e_i^* \otimes f_j^*$ to the functional taking $e_k \otimes f_l$ to $\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}$, which is the dual basis of the basis $(e_k \otimes f_l)$ of $V \otimes W$. So it sends a basis to a basis.

(ii) By the universal property, bilinear forms on $V$ correspond to linear functionals on $V \otimes V$, and this correspondence is a linear isomorphism $B(V) \cong (V \otimes V)^*$. Combine it with (i) for $W = V$.
:::

:::note
Part (ii) agrees with the isomorphism $B(V) \cong \Hom(V, V^*)$, $b \mapsto \varphi_b$, of Theorem [9.1.8](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#theorem-9-1-8). Proposition [9.8.10](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-10) with $W = V^*$ gives $\Hom(V, V^*) \cong V^* \otimes V^*$, and the form $b(v, w) = \ell(v) m(w)$ has $\varphi_b(v) = b(v, \cdot\,) = \ell(v)\, m$, which corresponds to $\ell \otimes m$. So both routes from $B(V)$ to $V^* \otimes V^*$ give the same isomorphism.
:::

:::note
The dual map also has a description in terms of tensors. Chaining isomorphisms, $$\Hom(V, W) \cong V^* \otimes W \cong W \otimes V^* \cong W^{**} \otimes V^* \cong \Hom(W^*, V^*),$$ using Proposition [9.8.10](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-10), the swap of Proposition [9.8.8](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-8)(i), the isomorphism $W \cong W^{**}$ of Theorem [6.2.19](/notes/math-55a/6-2-duality#theorem-6-2-19) on the first factor, and Proposition [9.8.10](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-10) again. Follow a rank-one map $\varphi(v) = \ell(v) w$ through the chain: it goes to $\ell \otimes w$, then to $w \otimes \ell$, then to $\ev_w \otimes \ell$ (where $\ev_w(\alpha) = \alpha(w)$), and finally to the map $\alpha \mapsto \alpha(w)\, \ell$. That map is $\varphi^t$, because $\varphi^t(\alpha) = \alpha \circ \varphi = \alpha(w)\, \ell$. Both ends of the chain are linear in $\varphi$, and rank-one maps span $\Hom(V, W)$, so the composite sends every $\varphi$ to its dual map $\varphi^t$. This is a construction of the transpose that uses no bases.
:::
